column1: What is the symmetric differential form of a first-order ODE, and what geometric question does it ask?
column2: $M(x,y)\,dx + N(x,y)\,dy = 0$. It asks: along what curves does the 1-form $\omega = M\,dx + N\,dy$ vanish, treating $x$ and $y$ symmetrically as coordinates on the plane.

column1: State the Picard-Lindelöf theorem's Lipschitz condition and the resulting existence interval half-width $h$.
column2: Lipschitz: $|f(x,y_1)-f(x,y_2)| \le L|y_1-y_2|$ for all $(x,y_1),(x,y_2)\in R$. The solution exists uniquely on $(x_0-h, x_0+h)$ where $h = \min(a, b/M_f)$, with $M_f = \sup_R |f|$.

column1: Describe the Picard iteration scheme used to constructively prove existence in Picard-Lindelöf.
column2: $y_0(x) = y_0$, $y_{n+1}(x) = y_0 + \int_{x_0}^{x} f(t, y_n(t))\,dt$. This sequence is shown to be Cauchy in $C([x_0-h,x_0+h])$ under the sup norm, converging to the unique fixed-point solution.

column1: Why does the equivalence $y(t) = y_0 + \int_{t_0}^t f(s,y(s))\,ds$ matter for existence proofs?
column2: It reformulates the differential equation as an integral equation, trading differentiation (which amplifies irregularities) for integration (a smoothing operation), enabling fixed-point/contraction mapping arguments via Banach's theorem.

column1: For an $n$-th order linear ODE $L[y] = f(x)$, what is the structure of the full solution set in terms of $\ker L$ and a particular solution $y_p$?
column2: $\text{Sol}(L[y]=f) = y_p + \ker L$ — an affine subspace of $C^n(I)$: a translate of the homogeneous solution subspace $\ker L$ by any single particular solution $y_p$.

column1: Prove why the difference of any two solutions of $L[y]=f$ lies in $\ker L$.
column2: If $L[y_1]=f$ and $L[y_2]=f$, then by linearity $L[y_1-y_2] = L[y_1]-L[y_2] = f-f = 0$, so $y_1-y_2 \in \ker L$.

column1: What defines an equilibrium point and a periodic orbit in the phase plane of an autonomous system $\dot x = f(x,y), \dot y = g(x,y)$?
column2: Equilibrium: $(x^*,y^*)$ with $f(x^*,y^*)=0$ and $g(x^*,y^*)=0$ (velocity vector vanishes). Periodic orbit: a nontrivial closed curve $\Gamma$ with $\varphi(t+T)=\varphi(t)$ for some finite $T>0$.

column1: Why must a system be autonomous for orbits to be well-defined as time-independent geometric objects?
column2: Autonomy means $f,g$ have no explicit $t$-dependence, so if $\varphi(t)$ solves the system, any time-translate $\varphi(t+c)$ also solves it — making the trajectory shape in the $(x,y)$-plane independent of the starting time.

column1: Define positively invariant, negatively invariant, and invariant sets under a flow $\phi_t$.
column2: $S$ is positively invariant if $\phi_t(S) \subseteq S$ for all $t\ge 0$; negatively invariant if the same holds for $t\le 0$; invariant if both hold.

column1: State the Laplace transform definition and its region of convergence condition for a function of exponential order.
column2: $\mathcal{L}\{f\}(s) = F(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt$. It converges absolutely for $\text{Re}(s) > \alpha$ where $|f(t)| \le Me^{\alpha t}$; this half-plane is the ROC, bounded by the abscissa of convergence $\sigma_c$.

column1: Why do Laplace and Fourier transforms 'algebraize' differential equations?
column2: They map differential operators into multiplication operators in the transform domain — the domains where these linear operators become diagonal (spectral/eigenfunction representation), reducing differentiation to scalar multiplication by $s$ (or $i\omega$).

column1: For $Au_{xx} + Bu_{xy} + Cu_{yy} + \dots = G$, what is the discriminant and how does it classify the PDE?
column2: $\Delta = B^2 - 4AC$. $\Delta < 0$: elliptic; $\Delta = 0$: parabolic; $\Delta > 0$: hyperbolic. This classifies which directions can carry discontinuities and how Cauchy data propagates (characteristics).
